claims.text: Demanding mechanical loading at elevated temperature increases atomic mobility in a single-phase high-entropy alloy.
Stress-enhanced atomic mobility drives localized elemental or trace-impurity segregation.
Localized segregation leads to the formation of brittle precipitates.
The newly formed phases reduce plastic deformation and toughness and thereby promote brittle fracture.
The initial alloy is a homogeneous single-phase solid solution with a uniform elemental distribution.
The initial alloy has high ductility and toughness.
Temperatures of approximately 600–800°C promote enhanced diffusion and segregation during demanding loading.
Brittle precipitates or intermetallic phases form preferentially at grain boundaries or stress-concentration sites.
Trace interstitial impurities can promote phase segregation during high-temperature exposure.
Trace impurity interstitials encourage formation of alpha-titanium precipitates in Ti-V-Nb-Ta aged at 700°C.
Mechanical stress can directly drive elemental segregation and local phase decomposition.
The precipitates act as stress concentrators.
Mechanically loaded samples will show less work hardening than the as-cast or as-processed baseline.
Mechanically loaded samples will show lower fracture toughness than the baseline.
Mechanically loaded samples will contain newly formed brittle precipitates detectable by microscopy.
Thermal aging of Ti-V-Nb-Ta at 700°C causes progressive softening because segregation depletes strengthening interstitials from the matrix.
The proposed behavior may not occur at low temperature or low strain rate.
Failure to observe statistically significant precipitate formation or a measurable toughness reduction in both standard-impurity and purified loaded samples would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: High-strain-rate loading is presented as a condition that promotes diffusion-driven segregation, while low-strain-rate conditions are excluded. This is mechanistically inconsistent without further justification because slower loading ordinarily provides more time for diffusion and precipitation.

The hypothesis predicts reduced work hardening, reduced toughness, and brittle fracture from brittle precipitates, whereas the cited evidence reports progressive softening caused by depletion of interstitial solid-solution strengthening and does not establish brittle precipitates, toughness loss, or fracture.
